articles.title: The Hollow Egalitarianism of LA's Revamped Art Museum
articles.author: Todd Cronan
articles.content: Peter Zumthor, the architect of the controversial new Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA), wants to make one thing very clear : that “this building never looks down on you.” His sentiments are vaguely populist: the building “should be open to the people.” It’s a building type, he says , that “treats everybody equal” and “lets you have your opinion. Follow your own path.” Michael Govan, the equally controversial museum director who has steered this project since its inception in 2006, mirrors the architect’s vision: “You make your own path, you decide” where to go. The gallery guide is called “ Wander .” The former building, designed in 1965 by William Pereira, arranged works along chronological, geographic, and cultural lines, creating a multifloor, “hierarchical” structure. The new museum is organized across a single level elevated thirty feet in the air around four major bodies of water: the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific oceans, and the Mediterranean Sea. The 347,500-square-foot structure made of raw, unpigmented, board-formed concrete contains 110,000 square feet of display space and exhibits about 2,500 pieces of ancient and modern art, mixing new and old, high and low, East and West, and everything in between. At a cost of $720 million (and rising), the design was funded with a mix of sources from Los Angeles County and a few ultrawealthy megadonors. If there is one point that is stressed in every press release and architectural statement, it’s the idea that the “building de-emphasizes structural hierarchies.” One story tall, it has no high or low, no front or back. Govan speaks of a “mingling of objects and influences ever on the move,” a space “where you have inherently baked in it these areas of crossings, connections, diasporas.” He describes his vision as creating “an equitable organization of cultures, equally accessible” to all. A New Yorker puff piece makes the design’s basic aim explicit: “The idea was to abolish the hierarchies inherent in the old museums, which offered prime real estate to European painting and shunted other cultures and their artifacts aside.” Since its unveiling in 2013, the building has received an inordinate amount of criticism, some of it deserved, some not. The core concerns focus on a few areas including reduced gallery capacity (11,000 fewer square feet of exhibition space), less flexible spaces (the galleries are fixed), disorienting navigation with minimal labeling, lack of public input in the process, and massive cost. No doubt these are significant issues, but they don’t address what I take to be the most glaring problem: a romantic fantasy of the laborer as craftsman, one that bears no resemblance to the lived reality of workers today. The Raw and the Slick Zumthor and museum management defend the price tag by pointing to the fact that the building is intended to last forever. Zumthor took his cue from the “primordial quality of the tar pits” adjacent to the site. The concrete structure “should look old, excavated rather than superimposed — something that ‘feels like it was there forever and should be there forever.’” As Zumthor sees it , the problem with most architecture is its “slickness” — his catchall term for the consumerist worldview he despises — and he fashions himself by contrast as a simple artisan. As a critique of capitalism, “slick” is empty; it is about as sophisticated as thinking the problem with rich people is their McMansions. Zumthor sees the building as a challenge to the slickness that Los Angeles embodies. He is on record describing the city with a world-class cliché: “green lawns and bushes in the front yards of the houses look as if they were made of plastic.” Rather than a manufacturer of glossy cubes, Zumthor offers himself as a simple laborer, a common man of the people. “The German word Baumeister,” he says , “is a beautiful word. When you call me a Baumeister , it will make me happy.” He is a simple craftsman “without a diploma.” He “trusts non-architects more than he trusts architects.” Yet it is hard to imagine a more abstracted fantasy of labor than Zumthor’s. He speaks of the objects in the museum as displaced peoples, as objects that “speak,” if only we had ears to listen. Zumthor shows remarkable contempt for educators. Our ears are blocked up with the voices of “schoolteachers pinning everything down.” He hopes “there won’t be any tags” placed on the works by these repressive schoolteachers. So far, he has succeeded: his walls are stripped clean of nearly all information. His antidote to the schoolteachers and the slicksters is an army of (partially undocumented) laborers, whom he fantasizes as simple artisans plying their trade. From the beginning, he “imagined Mexican workers doing the ground” of the museum (a concrete artwork entitled Feathered Ground ), “something done by hand. Indigenous knowledge, people who have been there for a long time.” Obviously Zumthor does not mean these workers have lived for a “long time” in the area but rather that they carry in their blood an attachment to ancient soil — that their indigenous experience can give the “homeless” objects their voices back. The objects in LACMA’s collection were deracinated, Zumthor explains, cut loose from their contexts and histories. “I think this could be my task, to create a new home, a temporary home for these homeless pieces,” he concludes. Needless to say, his concern is not about such crass material things as wages, labor practices, or worker protections but rather with “how labor is hidden.” How these indigenous workers can show Americans “respect for tools, for work.” His aesthetic attraction to cracks — evident throughout the museum — is an expression of his desire to express labor rather than “conceal it.” Zumthor imagines that “revealing” labor rather than “concealing” it serves some unspecified political purpose. Architecture as Anti-Hierarchy Zumthor belongs to a long tradition that treats architecture as a critique of hierarchy and an embrace of the spiritual ideal of the laborer. Walter Gropius, in his famous 1919 Bauhaus Program, announced his desire to “create a new guild of craftsmen without the class distinctions that raise an arrogant barrier between craftsman and artist!” For the Bauhaus generation, breaking down the walls between classes was the highest form of political achievement. Its architects were inspired by the infamous utopian writer and romantic antiauthoritarian Paul Scheerbart, who fantasized a world where “kings walk with beggarmen, artisans walk with men of learning.” For Scheerbart, the craftsman had no interest in the debased socialist ideal of improved conditions. “New social welfare organizations, hospitals, inventions, or technical innovations and improvements,” Scheerbart proclaimed, will not “bring new culture” — only a new architecture could. Neither Scheerbart nor Gropius had any interest in ridding the world of either beggars or kings, only in fostering mutual respect between them and, by the same stroke, naturalizing their class positions. Scheerbart’s anti-hierarchical program shaped a range of influential practices including Bruno Taut’s The City Crown of 1920. Taut’s “non-political socialism” sought to “bridge every gap between fighting classes.” Taut sought “a better future, in which man will stand with mankind . . . without the barriers of the classes.” Like Zumthor, Taut regarded “comfort” (his version of “slickness”) as capitalism’s overarching vice. “Good Living, Education — knife and fork, railways and bathrooms, what do those bring us?” he wondered. Nothing but “guns, bombs, instruments for killing!” The problem was not that the world was full of rich and poor, capitalists and laborers, but how these groups saw each other. His aim was to preserve those differences while ridding the world of the “arrogant” boundaries between them. Erich Baron, another “socialist” writing in The City Crown , saw all the people of earth united in their “suffering,” including “emperor, king, gentleman, peasant, burgher, and beggar.” It went without saying that “cultural progress” could not “be measured by how the poor climb into higher classes.” Here the architects were in harmony with contemporary fascist economists, who, alongside Baron, insisted that “the notable increase of wages was not accompanied by greater civilization.” The Reality of Labor at LACMA The Bauhaus vision of anti-hierarchy is alive and well in Zumthor’s design and in the visual display. Contemporary museum directors, curators, and architects hold hands in their united vision of a world without barriers and in their celebration of craft labor — just so long as you don’t have to pay those craftsmen a living wage. According to the Los Angeles Times , more than 25 percent of full-time LACMA workers do not make a living wage, a figure that spikes to 69 percent for entry-level employees. In December 2025, over three hundred LACMA workers formed a union, LACMA United (affiliated with the American Federation of State, Municipal and County Employees District Council 36), seeking better pay, expanded benefits, and more transparency. Workers pushed for unionization to address what they described as widespread burnout, high turnover, and inadequate compensation as they faced pressure to complete the David Geffen Galleries. In October 2025, Govan and museum leadership roundly declined to voluntarily recognize the union (putting them at odds with other recent unionization efforts at LA cultural institutions such as the Museum of Contemporary Art and the Academy Museum). Museum management instead insisted on a formal election before recognizing the union. Following a secret-ballot election, an overwhelming 96 percent of participating LACMA employees voted in favor of unionizing. In a letter to management, LACMA United spelled out what they saw as the basic contradiction between the cultural critique of hierarchy and the capitalist reinforcement of class barriers: We celebrate LACMA’s reimagining of the encyclopedic museum, presenting a more interconnected and inclusive narrative of artistic expression. As the museum evolves, we believe that this vision should extend beyond rethinking hierarchies of display to include prioritizing the people who bring its mission to life. LACMA exemplifies a larger trend in museum design in which rethinking hierarchies of display serves as a smokescreen for exploiting the people who bring the mission to life.

articles.title: Building Our Own Power: An Interview with “Unions of Our Own” author Daniel Gross
articles.author: Midwestern Socialist -- Chicago DSA
articles.content: The following is an interview conducted by San Francisco Bay Area labor and social movements authors and organizers Robert Ovetz and James Tracy. They spoke with Daniel Gross about his new book Unions of Our Own: Eight Building Blocks to Change Work and the World (Haymarket Books, 2026). This interview has been edited for structure and clarity. How did you get involved with the workers movement? I worked at Borders Book and Music when I was really young. The pay, the hours, and the disrespectful treatment from some managers aggravated me. I figured the thing to do was reach out to unions, which I did. My coworkers and I started doing meetings, but all the while I was fighting with management solo, which of course was a mistake. No plot twist here, Borders soon fired me. So I didn’t get very far in my first effort, but it holds a great significance for me. It gave me my start in unionism. And it planted the seed to become obsessed with what causes victory in union campaigns. Fast forwarding a bit, I started working at Starbucks in 2003. I got to take part in the formation of a powerful labor union there, the IWW Starbucks Workers Union, which changed my life and many others. It also helped break new ground in the labor movement in two ways: one, workers organizing themselves, and two, the campaign demonstrated that those who had called the fast food and retail sectors “unorganizable” were mistaken. The seeds we contributed in both those respects have sprouted greatly in the last ten or so years. That campaign was high-profile, and it started a process which continues to this day of connecting with workers from diverse industries and accompanying them on their campaigns. I also started writing with my late mentor, Staughton Lynd, with whom I co-authored Labor Law for the Rank & Filer: Building Solidarity While Staying Clear of the Law (PM Press, 2008) and S olidarity Unionism at Starbucks (PM Press, 2011), the latter along with the great labor artist Tom Keough, also now departed. And I worked for well over a decade as a founding organizer of Brandworkers, a worker center of immigrant food manufacturing workers and one of the founding organizations of the Food Chain Workers Alliance. Those experiences again contributed to this blessing of having many liberatory workers get in touch with me and getting to be in movement with them. Twenty-five years of organizing at my own jobs and being in close movement with many others at their jobs helped lead to the lessons and analysis of Unions of Our Own — along with careful study of historical campaigns. During this time, I learned that it is coworkers in workplaces and industries who are best positioned to design and refine unions to meet their needs. And it takes a complete model to win, which consists of eight fundamental building blocks. There are the four foundational building blocks. The first is “Constituency,” which is the scope of coworkers you will organize among as well as secondary constituents who can help you come together and amplify your power when you do. Constituency is one of the most fiery questions in labor history and remains so today. The “Problem” building block deals with the issues or unmet needs weighing on you the most, on the job and beyond it. “Solution” is the type of union you’ll build, the affiliation choice you make, and the benefits you’ll create through your solidarity to take on the identified problems. “Strategy” is the 800-pound gorilla of a union model, the power to win your union solution. Once you have that foundation, you turn your attention to the four structure and growth building blocks. “Mechanism” is how you hold or codify your gains. It’s a building block with huge importance for the character and performance of a labor union, and for social change as a whole. “Structure” is about having a union that coworkers control. “Funding” is what your union needs and you can get it; how you get it matters a ton for the responsiveness and fighting spirit of your union. Finally, the “Metrics” building block measures what matters most in your model to learn what’s working and to help ensure you are honoring your union’s values. The book helps readers use the building blocks to maximize the chance at union victory, through bullet-pointed decision-making factors, many examples from contemporary campaigns, colorful and often hidden labor history, as well as my own stories. What is the main argument about the state of the workers movement in your new book Unions of Our Own ? I’ve surprised some folks when I’ve said I’m optimistic, that this is a far greater time for unionism than when I came of age in the economy at Borders around the turn of the century. While uneven, there’s been tremendous working class activity and a turn towards unionism in the last ten or so years in the United States. It is amazing, and there is much to celebrate. At the same time, unionism has not grown overall in that period and the collective worker power it takes to take on oligarchy and fascism is nowhere near sufficient. One of the things the book argues against is the tendency to say there is a method or technique that exists and we just need to execute the hell out of it with great discipline and then we can win in every geography and in every industry. Method and technique are very important and there are some great ones which I do share in the book. But the truth is that there is no cookie-cutter recipe that exists for workers to be able to meet their needs in full, honor their values, and advance their vision of the world in all contexts. On the other hand, it doesn’t make sense to attempt to start with a blank slate. That cuts you off from other working class wisdom and denies you a framework to your insights to the surface and test them. In conjunction with that framework, the tools to use it, and the validated moves our forbearers have made, my hope for the book is to make a small contribution to help coworkers maximize their chance of victory. What is your analysis of the role of unions in capitalism? Let me start with the two poles on either end. One is that unions are either never able to take on capitalism, they’ll always stabilize it to some extent. The other pole is that unions are always a meaningful check on capitalism. One of the essential points in the book is that there is a back-and-forth relationship between union visions and union models. If you have a liberatory vision, but your model is not in accord with it, the model will drag it down. Sometimes this will happen right away, sometimes it takes place over time. On the other hand, you can have a model that nourishes and advances a liberatory vision. One of the groups of readers whom Unions of Our Own is resonating with so far are workers who want to challenge capitalism and empire via a union. The book unpacks model choices that were made in the 1930s and consolidated in 1950 that tend to go against that. Workers have the right to make different choices, and I try to open up the field so they can consider doing so with confidence. My reading of history combined with what I’ve come to understand about the “structural and material basis” of unions gives me a strong conviction that some types of union models can help achieve a society that is led and operated by workers and communities and that can get us past capitalism. But without intentionality, it’s easy for a union to become an “agent of capital”— to borrow a phrase from a union staffer I quote in the book. What are the fundamental threats to and weaknesses of the workers movement today? The oligarchy is piling up more of our resources than ever. As neoliberalism unravels, large capital, led by tech capital and other segments of the capitalist class, is positioning fascism as an alternative that many are finding compelling. AI is sucking up all the knowledge workers have produced and subordinating workers with it. All the while it is piling up more capital for a small number of oligarchs. The main use of AI currently is to control, extract, kill, surveil, disinform, and disrupt. So there are many threats. Still, era after era it is workers on job sites, at companies, and in industries and communities who come up with union forms that work. This happens not in spite of, but because of challenges in the big picture economic, political, social, and technological environment. A weakness in the movement is not having enough space where workers have the opportunity to bring their collective wisdom to the surface and test it through struggle. The book, and even more so the growing community of people doing rank & file union building together, is an effort to expand that space. It is beyond inspiring to be part of that. What are the roadblocks standing in the way of union organizing in the U.S.? I’ve already mentioned the concentrated power of the oligarchy, so let me go elsewhere. One roadblock is that while many folks are trying to advance a liberatory labor movement, there are other forces in labor doing the opposite. Unions that are trying to grow their density via deals that disempower workers and shore up the power of capitalism. This is happening via legislative or other schemes between top union officials, company executives, and politicians to exchange bargaining rights for the right to strike, the right to meaningfully choose your union, and the right to democratically govern your union. Major visionary initiatives are being steamrolled by these efforts and many more will not be able to get off the ground in the first place because of this maneuvering. Those need to be called out and opposed. They need to be outmaneuvered and the only way to do it is a deep coworker to coworker solidarity structure in union models that work. One last thing is that it takes literally a single worker sitting down and starting to make a list of their coworkers to start the exploration of a union campaign. Any blockage, friction, or missing link for that worker to get started with confidence is a roadblock. None of these roadblocks is insurmountable by any means. This, again, is a superb time to consider the union-building journey. What needs to be done to reinvigorate the workers movement? More space and support of all kinds for workers is needed to design and refine their own union models. Solidarity Union Network (SUN) members and community participants have been hard at work on that. There is more union integration with movements and rank-and-file connection, as we saw during the successful effort to repel the ICE invasion of Minnesota in early 2026. We need more deep integration with each other as a global working class rather than as a national project, like we’re seeing among workers at Amazon. For folks in establishment unions, more work is of course needed to organize caucuses and boot out reactionary leaders, and that work is happening. But that’s not enough to avoid reverting to the status quo. You’ve got to collectively document and challenge the regressive parts of the union. Take the reform effort at the United Auto Workers (UAW) and at many other unions I could cite: these movements didn’t just organize a base and vote in a new leadership, as important as that is. It whittled down the management prerogatives clause to preserve strike rights to prevent plant closure. It changed the union constitution for direct elections of the president. It expanded the scope of autoworkers to seriously organize to include those in the American South. Its 2023 work stoppage innovated on the classic “whipsaw strike” to great effect, as I analyze in the labor strategy canon part of the book. Respectively, those are changes to the mechanism, union structure, constituency, and strategy building blocks of the UAW model. Those union model changes should inspire folks in other traditional unions just as much as the change of leadership. *** People fed up with work and imagining something different can find Unions of Our Own , free digital tools from the book, trainings, book talks, and confidential one-on-one support from SUN at unionsofourown.org . The post Building Our Own Power: An Interview with “Unions of Our Own” author Daniel Gross appeared first on Midwest Socialist .

articles.title: The Liberal Attempt to Contaminate Immigrant Solidarity with American Exceptionalism
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: by Ethan Rhodes Racial terror and removal have returned from the backroom to the front display here in the US, with the Trump Administration’s much-flaunted acceleration of crackdowns on internal immigrant communities – most of them Latin American or Caribbean. Since Trumpism has retaken executive office, interior deportations, immigrant arrests, and prolonged detentions have skyrocketed . The Trumpists have preempted and post-hoc justified the according breakup of families, brutality of ICE, and degrading standards of living in immigrant concentration camps with the propagation of a rhetorical climate of nativist and dog-whistle racist dehumanization. Rightfully, many working-class Americans of conscience have been in an uproar. Uprisings have occurred, and counteraction has been organized, from Los Angeles to Minnesota – and even here in Rochester. In customary duplicity of face and of word, however, the anti-socialist forces of liberalism have been attempting, to some success, to hijack the uproar. The liberals have moved to mold immigrant solidarity into a docile shape, which does not present a material threat to the social rule of capital or to the core of its deportation regime. On the rhetorical front, they have kept quiet about the draconian deportation politics of the Democratic presidencies – from Roosevelt to Biden – which they so exalt, and they have mischaracterized deportations as the result of the pure machination of one man in Trump and one party in the GOP, rather than as a dual mechanism of capital, to dupe labor into racial division and dispose of its surplus. On the tactical and strategical fronts, they have practiced dancing and holding carnivals before immigrant detention centers rather than really closing them down, and they have limited the question of long-term change to operational reform of the deportation regime at the expense of its abolition. This article sticks to the rhetorical front of the hijacking, the contamination, with the goal of bringing attention to one of its more overlooked aspects. In addition to exonerating themselves and the capitalist mode of production through attributing immigration crackdowns only to the Trumpists, the liberals have invented a “pro-immigrant” appeal which centers a supposed “national character” of the US. As early as 2024, the Democratic National Convention wrote in a statement , “America is a nation of immigrants… Their sacrifices and belief in the unlimited possibilities of the American Dream help propel our nation to adhere to our foundational ideas of opportunity and equality.” For another example, the California Democratic Party states on its website , “California is the most diverse state in the nation and reflects the foundation of America’s strength… We know that we can strengthen America’s borders while upholding our values by honoring the tradition of providing a safe place for immigrants seeking a life of freedom and opportunity.” Leader of Senate Democrats Chuck Schumer introduces his immigration position on his website, “We are a nation of immigrants…” In such an appeal, immigration crackdowns should not be opposed simply because they are inhumane or because the mixing of cultures is benign, but because they are specifically contradictory to “the essence of America.” Diversity and the extension of refuge to the needy do not improve America; they improve only America. They are specifically and uniquely American, and simply that is why immigration crackdowns are wrong. Socialists must oppose such a sensationalist-nationalist “melting pot” exceptionalization of the US. Of course, we must maintain a pro-immigrant stance and work. But rhetorically, we must ground them not on a “special national trait,” but on the moral and practical need for constant solidarity with other regular, working people, regardless of their national origin or phenotype. For one, the flat truth is that diversity and immigration are not unique to the US. Rudimentary geography reveals that. Almost all countries are “diverse.” China – likely our bourgeoisie’s greatest current specter – is home to Han, Zhuang, Hui, Mongolians, Tibetans, Uyghurs, and many other ethnic groups. Mexico – one of our two most intimate neighbors – has as a fundamental process in its history the mixing of cultures, namely Indigenous and Spanish, called “mestizaje.” Iran – against which our bourgeoisie’s military has been aggressing – is a mosaic of Persians, Gilakis, Azerbaijanis, Kurds, Arabs, Balochis; Muslims, Christians, Jews, Zoroastrians, Baha’is. Furthermore, many countries are diverse specifically through formative immigration, if one could call it that. Into Australia have come British, Irish, other Europeans, Chinese, South Asians, West Asians, and North Africans; into South Africa Dutch, British, other Europeans, Indigenous Africans from the north, and South Asians; into Argentina Spanish, Italians, Irish, French. Additional examples abound. Flat truths asserted, note that all those last three countries with histories of formative immigration are settler-colonial. Would not congratulating Australia – through its holocaust of the Aboriginals; South Africa – through its apartheid Boer and British occupation; Argentina – through its government-commissioned whitening – for having achieved “diversity through immigration” be a poor choice of words? The liberal “pro-immigrant” exceptionalization of the US is precisely that. It obscures the nature of diversity and “immigration” in the history of the US. The first “immigrants” to this country were world-eating land robbers from the British Isles, and the close seconds were involuntary, brought on ships from Africa. The exceptionalization whitewashes such white supremacy and imperialism as simple “immigration,” which socialists can never do. We must stand with immigrants on the basis of the fraternity of the international working class, and with that comes open admission of, and advocacy for restitution for, a past without such a fraternity. As for the immigrant groups which have come after – Mexicans, Chinese, Italians, Ashkenazi Jews, and so on – they have never been accepted into the US because it is some benevolent land of milk and honey with golden streets and warm arms ready to embrace, as the poet Emma Lazarus naively rhetoricated in her famous ode to the Statue of Liberty, “huddled masses yearning to breathe free.” They have been allowed in – and have been accordingly excluded – only insofar as mostly white-owned capital has sought cheap labor, and duped its white labor into racial paranoia. These later immigrants have been packed onto farm trucks, used as fodder on railroads and in factories and sweatshops, forced to endure demeaning hours, workplace tyranny, sweltering heat and biting cold, low pay, and slums as homes. When they have rebelled, they have been fired, beaten, lynched, deported, or excluded. We can celebrate their endurance without proffering a false honor to the country which only begrudgingly took them in to exploit them. Finally and doubtless most importantly, the telos of the “melting pot” exceptionalization is to imbue the American working class with arrogance, to make it self-congratulatory for an open-door diversity which never was. As Marx and Engels wrote, a precondition of socialism is advocacy for the fraternity of workers of all peoples of the world, which requires national modesty in favor of the fervor of class loyalty. The exceptionalization which the liberals push is not customary pride in the productive communion of different cultures in a country. It is supremacist nationalist emotionality: “America is the best country for immigrants; that is why the acceleration of crackdowns is wrong.” It is tacit denial of a bad white-supremacist, settler-colonial past, and bourgeois arrogance. Socialists can stand against nativism and racism – in all their forms, whether overt or covert and liberal – and dare to struggle for immigrants persecuted, as they should for all members of the working class, without sacrificing national modesty and internationalism. These alone make for a united working class at home and abroad, which, in precisely its unity, can unlock the achievement of socialism. When they are sidelined or dropped for patriotic attachment to the bourgeois nation as some exceptional character, the socialist cause is disarticulated. The post The Liberal Attempt to Contaminate Immigrant Solidarity with American Exceptionalism first appeared on Rochester Red Star .

articles.title: Socialist Francesca Hong Could Be Wisconsin’s Next Governor
articles.author: Francesca Hong
articles.content: Wisconsinites have a high-stakes decision to make in the Democratic gubernatorial primary on August 11: whether or not to elect the first socialist governor in the state’s history, Francesca Hong. A Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) member and college dropout who, before she was elected to the state legislature in 2020, had worked as a dishwasher, line cook, bartender, and chef, Hong is the front-runner in the race. Many voters remain undecided , though this number seems to have shrunk significantly in recent days. She has the support of a number of progressive organizations and unions across the state. And she seems to be outworking her opponents, none of whom have generated as much enthusiasm, assembled as many statewide volunteers, or received as much money from Wisconsin donors. A daughter of Korean parents who immigrated to the United States in the 1980s, Hong grew up in Wisconsin. If she wins, she will become part of her home state’s rich socialist history. From 1905 to 1945, the Wisconsin legislature passed over five hundred pieces of legislation authored by socialists, and Wisconsinites sent a socialist to Congress and elected socialist mayors. In 2011, when Hong was in her early twenties, conservative Republican Governor Scott Walker gutted the state and wrenched it rightward, depriving tens of thousands of workers of long-held collective bargaining rights, crippling unions through a right-to-work law, and slashing aid to local schools and governments. Hong’s parents were public sector workers, and her family joined mass protests against Act 10, the 2011 law Walker championed that stripped most public sector workers of their collective bargaining rights. We are now in what Hong calls a “movement moment.” Democratic socialists have won numerous races throughout the country. In June, New York City DSA, of which I’m a member, won nine out of the ten races in which it endorsed, including two congressional primaries. In western New York, DSA-backed Buffalo attorney Adam Bojak won a state assembly seat, and DSA member and Syracuse-based county legislator Maurice “Mo” Brown beat out one of the longest-serving Democrats in central New York for a seat in the state legislature. Brown’s opponent and allied groups outspent him five to one. Democratic ⁠socialist Melat Kiros toppled a fifteen-term congresswoman in the primary in a district that includes Denver, Colorado; democratic socialist Chris Rabb won a primary for a House seat in Philadelphia; and democratic socialist Janeese Lewis George is poised to become the mayor of Washington, DC. Some fear that running a democratic socialist like Hong in a state as politically mixed as Wisconsin will hand the governor’s race to Tom Tiffany, the presumptive Republican nominee. But lately it seems that running as a democratic socialist — and earning a DSA endorsement — can help candidates more than it hurts them. Hong has been endorsed by a number of Wisconsin DSA chapters, including Madison, Milwaukee, and Northeast Wisconsin. The Democratic Party establishment is deeply worried about these developments. Their preferred candidates are failing to catch fire with voters, and top Democratic officials and consultants are panicking. Just a few weeks ago, desperate to stop Hong, they were urging candidates and voters to coalesce around Lieutenant Governor Sara Rodriguez. Rodriguez has since dropped out amid a scandal over her ex–campaign manager’s financial mismanagement, and Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley (also known as “ Dirt McGirk ”), who had dropped out to back Rodriguez, is back in with Gov. Tony Evers’s blessing. Now that the establishment is lining up behind Crowley, he is gaining in the polls but still lags Hong. If elected, Hong has vowed to enact universal childcare and paid leave, tax the rich to better fund public schools, lower health care costs and expand Medicaid, provide free school meals to students statewide, establish a state-run public bank, and implement a moratorium on data center construction. Like her predecessor Scott Walker, she could transform the state for decades to come — this time, in a way that could return power to millions of working-class people in Wisconsin and beyond. Jacobin contributor Raina Lipsitz recently sat down with Hong to discuss those possibilities. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Raina Lipsitz You’re serving your third term as a state legislator. What made you want to run for governor? Francesca Hong This is a historic moment for our state. It’s a movement moment, and a time where more and more working-class people are realizing that the economy is very much rigged against us. We need a government that is willing to make government a force of good, to help people get more democratic control of the economy. Raina Lipsitz I live in New York. I was involved in Zohran Mamdani’s mayoral campaign, and I remember when Zohran started running, he did this video where he asked Donald Trump supporters in the Bronx, “What made you vote for Trump? What are you frustrated about?” I know you’ve done similar outreach. What do you think is important to understand about folks who voted for Trump, and where are you seeing areas of common ground between you as a socialist and people who supported the president? Francesca Hong I think people are feeling screwed over by their government and rightfully frustrated. We’re finding common ground on raising wages, taxing the ultrarich, talking to small business owners who know that megacorporations are getting tax breaks and credits while we’re struggling to keep our main streets open. We’re the only campaign to support a moratorium on the construction of data centers; many people support this position, and I think it has a lot to do with feeling like they’re losing control of their communities. Big Tech and surveillance are coming in to ruin their way of life. This is a lot about people wanting to be a part of big change. Raina Lipsitz Tell me about the campaign you’ve built. Francesca Hong We’re a community- and grassroots-powered campaign. We’ve built this incredible volunteer community that people are bringing joy into. Folks are hosting playdates, dance parties, talking about why it’s so important to get out and vote on August 11 and November 3 and demand more of their government. Big money in politics is a challenge. Fundraising is always a challenge. But we’re proud to have the most individual donations and unique donors. I think that shows that this is an opportunity for the many and not just the money. The working class is the majority, and we should have a bigger voice in our government and be the ones to shape the policy. The majority of working-class folks here in Wisconsin want to feel safe, to be able to afford to live. No one should be too poor to live in our state. Good wages, great public schools, free childcare, quality health care, especially in our rural areas — that’s what the majority want. Raina Lipsitz You’ll be outspent, I’m sure. But what’s most difficult about breaking through with a message like yours? Francesca Hong I think it is breaking through. Things like health care, public education, lowering costs — we need to be building permanent affordability. We should be trying something new. And I think folks get caught up in labels and not solutions. People hold multitudes. I really struggle with folks shaming people who are working and living under a system that’s not serving them for who they may have voted for in the past. I’m talking to Trump voters [who agree that] it makes more sense that everyone should have health care, and that the millionaires and billionaires shouldn’t be paying a lower tax rate than working-class folks. Raina Lipsitz What do you see as the biggest stakes in this moment, in this election? Francesca Hong I keep going back to making government a force of good. Sixteen years of Republican rule and Democratic complacency has led to dysfunction and defunding of public services and state agencies. We have to make sure that the state is there when you need it, with social insurance programs that will make your life easier. When we have politicians who are not acting in the interests of working-class people, it leads to everyone out on their own. What’s most at stake is winning a Democratic trifecta in the state legislature, so that we can work together to write our democratic values into law. Public education, health care, and shared revenue are some of my top priorities, because I think that’s where we can make aggressive investments to change the material conditions of people’s lives the quickest. Raina Lipsitz Do you see Minnesota as a model? When they had a Democratic trifecta, they did a lot very quickly. How would you duplicate that success in Wisconsin? Francesca Hong It’s great to see what worked and what didn’t work with a slim majority in Minnesota. We want to maintain the majority when we have it, and that is going to require all of the state legislature, the executive branch, and all of our state agencies to work collectively. I want to see additional investment in agriculture. Both Minnesota and Wisconsin have a strong agricultural heritage, and our farmers are really struggling. I’d like to ensure that our agencies like the Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection, and the Department of Natural Resources are funded to make sure we’re helping folks navigate additional programs available from the state to help them, especially when Trump is implementing tariffs and jacking up fuel prices while our tax dollars are going to forever wars. Wisconsin can make sure that, regardless of zip code, you have support and opportunities to navigate whatever level of crisis you’re going through because of the federal government. Raina Lipsitz Only fourteen US states are run by women. Has gender been a factor in your campaign? Francesca Hong A lot of people I talk to are pretty excited to elect our first woman governor. I remind people who may be skeptical to look at where we are. We’ve only had male governors and a male-dominated legislature. Maybe it’s time to elect a woman. Raina Lipsitz How has being a child of immigrants affected your politics? Francesca Hong My parents came here to pursue education. At the time, Korea was also going through political upheaval. I take being a public servant very seriously. I prioritize sacrifice, service, and community. And I owned a restaurant for seven years. I still work in the service industry. I think the dishwasher is one of the most important people in a restaurant. In Wisconsin, we take care of our neighbors. Those are our values. Raina Lipsitz Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez famously was a bartender before she was elected to Congress. You’ve talked about working as a dishwasher and a line cook. What skills have you transferred from those jobs to the campaign? Francesca Hong Working collaboratively, understanding that every position in the restaurant is important and contributes to the success of having a good service. At Friday night service, you have everything from the host, who is the first person you may see, to the line cook, who is turning out the lights at the end of the night — everyone plays an important role. I’ve worked with a lot of chefs who may have had more ego, and I think it’s important to put that aside, especially in government. I’ve learned to out-hustle folks. I didn’t go to culinary school, so I had to make sure the chefs I was working for saw my work ethic, my willingness to learn, and to actively listen to people around me. I think service industry folks are built different, and you see the best and worst in humanity in restaurants and how people can treat each other. I’ve learned a lot about how important it is to treat people with respect and honor who they are. Raina Lipsitz You’ve mentioned that people are more than their labels. People are hung up on the democratic socialist label. Why do you use that term? Why not just run as a progressive? What’s important to you about defining yourself that way? Francesca Hong The word “democratic.” Being a democratic socialist means that my values are rooted in democracy, fairness, and human rights. It’s why I’ve been vocal in organizing, I’ve been vocal on Palestinian rights, and I’ve been fighting to have fair taxation, taxing the ultrarich and the megacorporations. I want everyone to have a say in what shapes their lives. The numbers are showing that especially our young people are supportive of democratic socialist policies. Bernie Sanders won seventy-one out of seventy-two counties here in Wisconsin in 2016. It’s more about the solutions than it is the labels. When I’m talking to folks on the trail about it, I go back to fully funded public schools. I go to the three Ps, popular things in our state that have socialist roots or socialist policies: the Green Bay Packers, public schools, and potholes. The Packers are a publicly owned football team; we have a constitutional obligation to ensure every child has a sound and good public education. And potholes — everyone’s thinking about potholes. They see them. They drive on the roads that we all pay for, and we need to be giving our local governments more money so that we can help them fix the roads, and that comes from distributing wealth, and that has to come with people paying their fair share of taxes. Raina Lipsitz When did you join DSA, and when did you start to think of yourself as a democratic socialist? Francesca Hong I didn’t really even know what community organizing was as a term; I’d read a little Saul Alinsky. To me, the label “community organizing” made more sense. It’s building relationships. When I joined DSA in 2020, it was because the things that they were fighting for and talking about were things that I align with when it comes to raising wages, racial justice, and fighting for working-class people and not the oligarchs. Being a member of DSA, and the community organizing it’s doing, is so important. Look at the work that DSA is doing on the ground. That is a big part of our campaign. We’ve already hit tens of thousands of doors and had thousands of conversations, and sometimes it’s more the messenger than just the message. And to have folks who identify however politically, but then to talk about free childcare, a data center moratorium, and fully funding our public schools — when you’re hearing it from your neighbor as opposed to a politician, it hits different. Raina Lipsitz Wisconsin has a rich socialist history, but it also has a history as a laboratory for the far right. How do you plan to reverse the structural damage that politicians like Scott Walker did to the social safety net and public institutions? And how do you do it in a way that’s not just going to reverse that damage, but solidify those gains so they can’t just be undone again in the next election? Francesca Hong Take Act 10 [the Scott Walker law which severely restricted public sector collective bargaining rights]. It’s not enough just to repeal Act 10. It should be in the state constitution that everyone has a right to collectively bargain or unionize. So putting a stake in it means let’s take it to the people, a ballot referendum question, and ask. If it’s in our constitution, it’s much harder to repeal. We still have an abortion ban on our books in the constitution that we should have repealed a long time ago. And then the funding piece. It’s important that these programs I introduced — I’m the lead author of Paid Leave for All, and the way that the program would work is very much like unemployment insurance, where it starts to pay for itself. [Hong introduced a bill that would expand Wisconsin’s family and medical leave law and establish a family and medical leave insurance program. Like the state’s unemployment insurance program, it would be funded by corporate taxes, which means payroll contributions from participating employers and employees would cover the program’s costs.] They know that it’s there when they need it, and it ends up being a program that can pay for itself and also ensure that folks have twelve to fourteen weeks of paid family or medical leave. Undoing structural damage comes with building something new that’s lasting, and that has to be both through funding, through statutes and our constitution, and in shifting the culture and the narrative around why we deserve these things. Raina Lipsitz There’s a lot of fear out there about electability. A lot of folks who say things like, “I really like what you’re saying, but I need to back the person who can win in the fall.” How do you address those fears? Francesca Hong The person who is most electable is the person who wins the most votes. When people fear that their neighbor may not be voting the same way they are because they’re scared of a candidate that they want to vote for but have hesitations about, then we’re never going to get the candidate that we want. That’s why organizing is so important, because it’s both telling and showing the power of a movement. We’re showing that, whether it’s with poll numbers, number of volunteers, the press that we’ve been getting. But also that these policies we’re fighting for have broad appeal to Republicans, independents, and moderates — there’s an opportunity to build the coalition that’s strong enough to win. And I’m going up against a candidate who is an election-denying traitor, a pedophile protector, someone who supports gutting health care from Americans and ripping food away from our kids, and an abortion ban nationwide. But I want folks to know, even if you don’t vote for me in the primary or in the general, I want you to have good health care and great schools. The electability question — you can combat that fear when you see community being built and folks talking about hope. Raina Lipsitz I’ve been thinking about a speech Zohran Mamdani gave before the primary election a year ago. He said , “The days of moral victories are over.” People were electrified by hearing someone say “I have a responsibility to you to win.” Is that something you think about? Do you see it in those terms? Francesca Hong We are running to win. I would not have come into the race if I didn’t think I could win. We are running to build power for working-class people, and we are running to deliver for Wisconsinites. This is about policy that will improve lives and make life easier for everyone in our state. I don’t think Democrats talk enough about power. We can’t be afraid of it. We have to reclaim it, and this is the opportunity for Wisconsin to do that, where we win the trifecta and move with urgency to respond to a time of crisis and chaos. I hear a lot about fighting Trump, but that also has to mean fighting for the people of Wisconsin by making sure the government gives them what they need to be able to take care of themselves, in a time where the regime does not care about you, Trump does not care about you. I want you to be able to take care of yourself, your loved ones, and your community. It’s about freedom and power, and that means Democrats have to win. Wisconsin’s a bellwether state. As goes Wisconsin, so goes the country. And, like Mayor Mamdani, we’re seeing across the state other election wins for democratic socialists and progressives. I think if we can do this at the statewide level, we’re going to change politics across the country.

articles.title: DFA – The Northeast Milk Monopoly
articles.author: Champlain Valley DSA
articles.content: Note: posts by individual GMDSA members do not necessarily reflect the views of the broader membership or of its leadership and should not be regarded as official statements by the chapter. Photo Credit: Glenn Russell/VTDigger Eighty of our neighbors, including fifty-five hard-working members of Teamsters 597, are losing their jobs. On June 17th, the Dairy Farmers of America announced plans to “idle” their Saint Albans City facility. The effects of this idling will be catastrophic and will ripple out across Vermont and the Northeast: dairy farms will be forced to shoulder the financial cost of transporting their raw milk to facilities in faraway New York or Massachusetts where it will be mixed with milk from other farms during processing; markets will see distribution and supply of their dairy products change; local companies that produce dairy products, including Ben and Jerry’s, will grapple with supply chain alterations and changes in milk quality; the plant itself on Federal Street will sit empty save a skeleton maintenance crew; and most importantly, eighty employees will become jobless. The decision follows years of DFA slowly undermining farmer co-operatives throughout the Northeast with anticompetitive, antitrust monopolization that’s left local farmers struggling to break even while DFA reaps the spoils. Now we’re all hung out to dry. Franklin County deserves better. Vermont deserves better. Our friends and neighbors, the hard-working members of Teamsters 597, deserve better. This isn’t the first time that DFA has engaged in antitrust action: a 2020 lawsuit filed against DFA by Food Lion LLC and the Maryland and Virginia Milk Producers Cooperation Association claims that “DFA’s conduct threatens to and will result in antitrust injury as it tends to and will substantially lessen competition.” A lawsuit filed closer to home in Vermont two years later, S.R.J.F Inc vs. DFA, argues that “over time, DFA has taken predatory and exclusionary actions to position itself as the sole conduit for Northeastern dairy farmers to get their raw milk to market, and to control Northeast raw milk processing capacity, the only market into which Northeast dairy farmers can sell their perishable product.” Other examples of DFA seizing regional dairy industries abound, and a dairy processing plant in Connecticut currently faces similar unexpected closure. This also isn’t the first time that DFA has proven itself a bad neighbor. Poor working conditions and unfair treatment from management led Teamsters 597 members to strike in October 2025, picketing on Federal Street late into the night. And ongoing discussions with Saint Albans City Council regarding rotten smells coming from the facility hit their most contentious note days before announcement of the plant's idling. DFA has proven itself more concerned with controlling our industry for their own gain than in supporting us, the dairy farmers, employees, and community members that call Vermont home. We all deserve better than an idling plant and hard-working union members without work, and we can’t allow monopolistic corporations with no regard for Vermont to strangle our dairy industry. We need legislators that use statute to create an economy where we can all succeed. We need laws that protect employees, to build strong participatory unions with greater investment from employees, and a pivot to co-operative worker-owned businesses over monolithic corporations without accountability. Our farmers and dairy workers deserve fair pay for the dairy products they produce instead of scraping by. Franklin County deserves better than a vacant DFA plant and the disruption of our dairy industry. And DFA needs to amend for the harm they’ve caused to our community and to the members of Teamsters 597.

articles.title: 400 Years of U.S. Pilgrimage: Why This Quaker is Walking Across the Country
articles.author: DSA Religion and Socialism Working Group
articles.content: On Wednesday, July 8, on day 54 of the National Peace Walk, two of us headed down Bradford Quarry Road in Alamance County, NC, toward Saxapahaw. The heat was oppressive. We had made a morning stop already at a church to refill our water reservoirs, taking a minute to tell a passerby about this nationwide pilgrimage that began in Brooklyn almost two months earlier. He remarked, as most tend to, that it seemed like a lot of walking. I tried, as I usually do, to downplay the physical challenge, as it is always made worthwhile by the spiritual nourishment of meeting with community at our destinations. Still, I had just bought a new set of insoles to replace the ones that I had walked to tatters, and I wasn’t sure how far this new two liters of hose water would get us. An hour later, Luther Livermon, a friend-to-be, slowed his car next to us and welcomed us to rest and refill at his house, a few yards down the road. When we arrived, we were officially introduced to Luther; his wife, Karen; and the two nurses who are her caretakers. Karen lives with dementia. Luther told us about his plan to eventually offer his 75-acre farm to Teepa Snow , a world-renowned specialist in care for those living with brain-change. Luther hoped that this offering would create a sanctuary for specialized care, as well as stewardship of the natural world, which could weather the impending changes of our society. He spoke on all of this unprompted, not aware yet that a core mission of our pilgrimage was to meet with communities working actively to create resilience through mutual aid in the United States. Luther also had posted signs along his farm’s frontage for the Preserve Alamance Coalition , an effort by Alamance County residents to halt the clearcutting of mature forest for construction of 1000 units of low-density housing by developers. A local friend and walk organizer, Krysten Voelkner, had coincidentally planned to meet us at the exact time we visited Luther’s farm, giving the two of them an opportunity to be introduced as neighbors and allies in the struggle to protect local forests and water. The simple, grounding activity of walking has led to many encounters like these. Our visit with those on Luther’s farm that morning was an affirmation that this project is one of making a path toward continual serendipity, walked by those who are ready to encounter it. Last fall, I was part of the organizing committee for the Quaker Walk to Washington , and the work that has continued from this act of public witness now has me on a pilgrimage bound for Minneapolis. Throughout my life, my tendency to be drawn toward egalitarian communities has kept me in overlapping circles of Quaker and socialist groups. Personal photo by author Since beginning pilgrimage work with Brooklyn Quakers in early 2025, I have literally and figuratively followed a tradition that is older than what is known now as the United States. Quakers have been walking pilgrimages on this continent for nearly four hundred years as an act of peace. This simple act continues to be an effective way to step outside of many oppressive, interconnected systems to meet with friends in true intention. Quakerism has always had much to offer fellow socialists. Our historic mode of governance prioritizes long, thoughtful discernment which necessarily resolves in consensus. Quaker governance serves as the basis for the theory of sociocracy . In what was then known as New Netherland, Peter Stuyvesant famously banned Quakers from practicing their religion . A 1657 petition called the Flushing Remonstrance was a call by residents of the borough for ratified religious liberty. Over a hundred years later, the petition inspired the Founders to include freedom of religion in the Bill of Rights, connecting Quaker society to this essential feature of spiritual freedom in the United States. The National Peace Walk 2026 follows this tradition of publicly expressing faith as an immovable societal foundation, one that weathers all periods of change. Walking to bring this good news to friends extends from a literal and metaphorical lineage that exists both on this continent, and throughout the world. Dozens of folks we have met along the way speak of the Camino de Santiago , currently experiencing the highest number of pilgrims since the 16th century. More recently, in our own country, a group of Buddhist monks walked 3,500 kilometers and gained international attention for the cause of peace and understanding. Their walk extended to Sri Lanka after the U.S. phase was finished. The tradition of pilgrimage in the United States in modern times has been upheld by a few notable figures, including Peace Pilgrim , who walked for nearly 30 years, crossing the United States seven times, speaking before crowds and on radio. According to her story, she rested when offered lodging, ate when offered food, and carried nothing except the clothes she wore. In the days before the United States. celebrated “America250,” the National Peace Walk finally crossed the North Carolina border, leaving only two days of walking to the next Quaker meeting in Raleigh. Those days in Virginia proved to be a challenge unlike the prior 300 miles between New York City and Washington. The heat and fatigue were factors, but the size and remoteness of Route 1 outside of Richmond were staggering at points. On this section, we could no longer count on a nightly station with Quakers, other faith groups, or communities of people activated toward building peace. We saw instead a kind of cultural blight: towns that had emptied after the dissolution of an unsustainable industry or the construction of I-95/85. In earlier days, when we might have stopped at some center of community for rest and water, there was now just a Wawa store, and then at a certain latitude, a Sheetz . We took our overnight rest on an abandoned porch or in the prohibitively expensive, soulless interior of a hotel room. The act of intentionally meeting with friends at times can feel utterly inaccessible without acquiescing to a number of oppressive systems, installed by the force of convenience. “America at 250” on its face would like to be a celebration of a unity among states, but the lived reality for most in the Covid-era is an encroaching stasis of isolation, even “post” lockdown. The recent work of pilgrimage by NYC Quakers has been a modern effort to transcend these divides and to meet with friends as companions and partners in the realization of a peaceful world. Our intention as walkers is to reach Minneapolis by November, in order to celebrate the work of residents of the Twin Cities to build resilience under the pressure of full-bore state violence. From where we stand now, in Boone, North Carolina, a walk to Minneapolis could seem like an untraversable distance. What is certain, as it has been revealed to us many times over at this point, is that applied faith shared by community will open a way. The serendipity of the journey will be found by those who set out to meet it.
